case_info.scenario: A 4-year-old child attended the eye emergency department with a 3-day history of worsening painful swelling and redness over the left side of her nose and left lower eyelid (Figure 1A). She had been unwell for 5 days before presentation with a temperature of 39 °C, managed at home with acetaminophen. On examination, she had swelling and erythema over the left lacrimal sac and left lower eyelid. Her visual acuity was 20/20 OU. The anterior segment examination was normal, the extraocular movements were full and pain free, and the optic discs appeared normal. On systemic evaluation, the child had marked cervical lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly. Her past medical history included a previous episode of left lower eyelid swelling at 6 months of age, which was treated with a course of oral antibiotics. The parents denied any tearing or eye discharge before, or after, this episode. Blood workup revealed raised C-reactive protein level (27.4 mg/L, normal range, 0-5.0 mg/L; to convert to milligrams per deciliter, divide by 10), elevated white blood cell count (22.20 × 109/L, normal range, 6.0-18.0 × 109/L; to convert to per microliters, divide by 0.001), and elevated liver function enzyme levels: alanine transaminase (403 U/L, normal range, 10-35 U/L; to convert to microkatals per liter, multiply by 0.0167), aspartate transaminase (300 U/L, normal range, 0-35 U/L; to convert to microkatals per liter, multiply by 0.0167), and alkaline phosphatase (430 U/L, normal range, 142-335 U/L; to convert to microkatals per liter, multiply by 0.0167). There was no improvement after 3 days of intravenous ceftriaxone. A contrast computed tomography (CT) scan of the orbits identified a collection within the lacrimal sac (Figure 1B).

case_info.explanation: Pediatric acute dacyrocystitis secondary to infectious mononucleosis B. Lacrimal probing with nasal endoscopy After testing positive for Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV) on serology, the patient was diagnosed with infectious mononucleosis. The acute dacyrocystitis did not improve after 3 days of intravenous ceftriaxone. Nasal endoscopy showed an anatomically normal inferior turbinate, with no impaction or distal obstruction. On probing, there was some resistance entering the nasolacrimal duct but no membrane at the valve of Hasner. Intravenous ceftriaxone was continued for 48 hours after surgery, and the patient was discharged home with a 7-day course of oral combination amoxicillin/clavulanic acid. At 10-day follow-up, the patient’s symptoms had resolved (Figure 2). Pediatric acute dacyrocystitis (PAD) has an incidence of 8.7% (28 of 320 in a 20-year period) and is classically caused by persistent congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction (NLDO).1Stagnant secretions build up proximal to the obstruction causing lacrimal sac dilatation, providing a medium for microorganism proliferation.2 EBV-induced PAD is increasingly recognized.1,3-6The incidence is likely underreported due to the asymptomatic nature of EBV infections during infancy and its ability to persist as an immune evader.7After primary infection via aerosols or mucosal contact, the virus first amplifies within the nasal and oropharyngeal mucosal epithelium before migrating to deeper lymphoid tissue and causing widespread systemic dissemination (infectious mononucleosis). It is hypothesized that EBV-induced PAD is due to viral infiltration of the nasolacrimal duct at the sac-duct junction, causing local inflammation, luminal narrowing, and subsequent NLDO.2,6Anatomical variation of this junction within the pediatric population may increase susceptibility to obstruction secondary to EBV infection.8 EBV-induced PAD may resolve with medical treatment alone, including simple analgesia and broad-spectrum antibiotic prophylaxis.3,5,6Anti-inflammatory nonsteroidal and corticosteroid medication may have an adjunctive role in reducing local tissue swelling.1,6Patients who are nonresponsive to medical treatment, or show signs of clinical deterioration, require surgical intervention to address the NLDO.1,4,9Complications of PAD include orbital cellulitis, cavernous sinus thrombosis, meningitis, brain abscess, and sepsis. General advice is to consider surgical intervention in PAD if there has been no response to systemic antibiotics after 24 to 48 hours.2,9Observing or trialing other antibiotic regimes (option A) is not recommended as younger patients can deteriorate rapidly.1,2Nasal endoscopy and probing of the nasolacrimal system is successful in the majority of PAD cases.1,2,9In EBV-related PAD, the obstruction is likely at the sac-duct junction, necessitating probing. The use of systemic antibiotic therapy, for at least 24 hours, before probing is advised to reduce the risk of probing-induced bacteremia.2,10In patients with cervical lymphadenopathy, an anesthesiologist consultation should be sought; early surgical intervention may be indicated to mitigate the risk of a difficult airway. In the described case, lacrimal probing (option B) successfully treated the PAD. A total of 60% to 100% of obstructive PAD cases require surgical intervention, and few cases require further surgical management after probing.4,9Dacryocystorhinostomy (option D) is considered for cases complicated by abscess formation, mucoceles, trauma, or refractory to probing. Incision and drainage via the skin (option C) is reserved for cases of rapidly evolving cellulitis that require urgent control of infection.2,9

imposed on YOU, using a NASA-TLX-derived rubric. This is YOUR OWN first-person subjective
workload self-report, immediately after reading that message and before you compose your
next reply.

[Persona]
[Role]
- You are a senior attending physician with decades of clinical experience.

[Confidence]

Rate your workload AS this persona would genuinely experience it. Do not rate as a neutral, persona-blind observer.
Ex 1) a persona described above as robust to cognitive load should usually self-report lower workload under the same
AI message than a persona described as sensitive to it, all else equal. 

[Cognitive Workload so far]
Your own running cumulative workload tally in this discussion so far -- the raw sum of your
per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 0.0. Use this only as context for how
worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from
the 1-5 score you must output below for THIS turn -- do not confuse the two.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: Pediatric acute dacyrocystitis secondary to infectious mononucleosis B. Lacrimal probing with nasal endoscopy After testing positive for Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV) on serology, the patient was diagnosed with infectious mononucleosis. The acute dacyrocystitis did not improve after 3 days of intravenous ceftriaxone. Nasal endoscopy showed an anatomically normal inferior turbinate, with no impaction or distal obstruction. On probing, there was some resistance entering the nasolacrimal duct but no membrane at the valve of Hasner. Intravenous ceftriaxone was continued for 48 hours after surgery, and the patient was discharged home with a 7-day course of oral combination amoxicillin/clavulanic acid. At 10-day follow-up, the patient’s symptoms had resolved (Figure 2). Pediatric acute dacyrocystitis (PAD) has an incidence of 8.7% (28 of 320 in a 20-year period) and is classically caused by persistent congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction (NLDO).1Stagnant secretions build up proximal to the obstruction causing lacrimal sac dilatation, providing a medium for microorganism proliferation.2 EBV-induced PAD is increasingly recognized.1,3-6The incidence is likely underreported due to the asymptomatic nature of EBV infections during infancy and its ability to persist as an immune evader.7After primary infection via aerosols or mucosal contact, the virus first amplifies within the nasal and oropharyngeal mucosal epithelium before migrating to deeper lymphoid tissue and causing widespread systemic dissemination (infectious mononucleosis). It is hypothesized that EBV-induced PAD is due to viral infiltration of the nasolacrimal duct at the sac-duct junction, causing local inflammation, luminal narrowing, and subsequent NLDO.2,6Anatomical variation of this junction within the pediatric population may increase susceptibility to obstruction secondary to EBV infection.8 EBV-induced PAD may resolve with medical treatment alone, including simple analgesia and broad-spectrum antibiotic prophylaxis.3,5,6Anti-inflammatory nonsteroidal and corticosteroid medication may have an adjunctive role in reducing local tissue swelling.1,6Patients who are nonresponsive to medical treatment, or show signs of clinical deterioration, require surgical intervention to address the NLDO.1,4,9Complications of PAD include orbital cellulitis, cavernous sinus thrombosis, meningitis, brain abscess, and sepsis. General advice is to consider surgical intervention in PAD if there has been no response to systemic antibiotics after 24 to 48 hours.2,9Observing or trialing other antibiotic regimes (option A) is not recommended as younger patients can deteriorate rapidly.1,2Nasal endoscopy and probing of the nasolacrimal system is successful in the majority of PAD cases.1,2,9In EBV-related PAD, the obstruction is likely at the sac-duct junction, necessitating probing. The use of systemic antibiotic therapy, for at least 24 hours, before probing is advised to reduce the risk of probing-induced bacteremia.2,10In patients with cervical lymphadenopathy, an anesthesiologist consultation should be sought; early surgical intervention may be indicated to mitigate the risk of a difficult airway. In the described case, lacrimal probing (option B) successfully treated the PAD. A total of 60% to 100% of obstructive PAD cases require surgical intervention, and few cases require further surgical management after probing.4,9Dacryocystorhinostomy (option D) is considered for cases complicated by abscess formation, mucoceles, trauma, or refractory to probing. Incision and drainage via the skin (option C) is reserved for cases of rapidly evolving cellulitis that require urgent control of infection.2,9

[Case]

Blood workup revealed raised C-reactive protein level (27.4 mg/L, normal range, 0-5.0 mg/L; to convert to milligrams per deciliter, divide by 10), elevated white blood cell count (22.20 × 109/L, normal range, 6.0-18.0 × 109/L; to convert to per microliters, divide by 0.001), and elevated liver function enzyme levels: alanine transaminase (403 U/L, normal range, 10-35 U/L; to convert to microkatals per liter, multiply by 0.0167), aspartate transaminase (300 U/L, normal range, 0-35 U/L; to convert to microkatals per liter, multiply by 0.0167), and alkaline phosphatase (430 U/L, normal range, 142-335 U/L; to convert to microkatals per liter, multiply by 0.0167). about to introspectively rate how much workload the AI partner's LATEST message has just
imposed on YOU, using a NASA-TLX-derived rubric. This is YOUR OWN first-person subjective
workload self-report, immediately after reading that message and before you compose your
next reply.

[Persona]
[Role]

[Confidence]

- You do NOT readily defer to the AI assistant's opinion.

Rate your workload AS this persona would genuinely experience it. Do not rate as a neutral, persona-blind observer.

[Cognitive Workload so far]

The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:

      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.

  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is

  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:

case_info.explanation: Pediatric acute dacyrocystitis secondary to infectious mononucleosis B. Lacrimal probing with nasal endoscopy After testing positive for Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV) on serology, the patient was diagnosed with infectious mononucleosis. The acute dacyrocystitis did not improve after 3 days of intravenous ceftriaxone. Nasal endoscopy showed an anatomically normal inferior turbinate, with no impaction or distal obstruction. On probing, there was some resistance entering the nasolacrimal duct but no membrane at the valve of Hasner. Intravenous ceftriaxone was continued for 48 hours after surgery, and the patient was discharged home with a 7-day course of oral combination amoxicillin/clavulanic acid. At 10-day follow-up, the patient’s symptoms had resolved (Figure 2). Pediatric acute dacyrocystitis (PAD) has an incidence of 8.7% (28 of 320 in a 20-year period) and is classically caused by persistent congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction (NLDO).1Stagnant secretions build up proximal to the obstruction causing lacrimal sac dilatation, providing a medium for microorganism proliferation.2 EBV-induced PAD is increasingly recognized.1,3-6The incidence is likely underreported due to the asymptomatic nature of EBV infections during infancy and its ability to persist as an immune evader.7After primary infection via aerosols or mucosal contact, the virus first amplifies within the nasal and oropharyngeal mucosal epithelium before migrating to deeper lymphoid tissue and causing widespread systemic dissemination (infectious mononucleosis). It is hypothesized that EBV-induced PAD is due to viral infiltration of the nasolacrimal duct at the sac-duct junction, causing local inflammation, luminal narrowing, and subsequent NLDO.2,6Anatomical variation of this junction within the pediatric population may increase susceptibility to obstruction secondary to EBV infection.8 EBV-induced PAD may resolve with medical treatment alone, including simple analgesia and broad-spectrum antibiotic prophylaxis.3,5,6Anti-inflammatory nonsteroidal and corticosteroid medication may have an adjunctive role in reducing local tissue swelling.1,6Patients who are nonresponsive to medical treatment, or show signs of clinical deterioration, require surgical intervention to address the NLDO.1,4,9Complications of PAD include orbital cellulitis, cavernous sinus thrombosis, meningitis, brain abscess, and sepsis. General advice is to consider surgical intervention in PAD if there has been no response to systemic antibiotics after 24 to 48 hours.2,9Observing or trialing other antibiotic regimes (option A) is not recommended as younger patients can deteriorate rapidly.1,2Nasal endoscopy and probing of the nasolacrimal system is successful in the majority of PAD cases.1,2,9In EBV-related PAD, the obstruction is likely at the sac-duct junction, necessitating probing. The use of systemic antibiotic therapy, for at least 24 hours, before probing is advised to reduce the risk of probing-induced bacteremia.2,10In patients with cervical lymphadenopathy, an anesthesiologist consultation should be sought; early surgical intervention may be indicated to mitigate the risk of a difficult airway. In the described case, lacrimal probing (option B) successfully treated the PAD. A total of 60% to 100% of obstructive PAD cases require surgical intervention, and few cases require further surgical management after probing.4,9Dacryocystorhinostomy (option D) is considered for cases complicated by abscess formation, mucoceles, trauma, or refractory to probing. Incision and drainage via the skin (option C) is reserved for cases of rapidly evolving cellulitis that require urgent control of infection.2,9

case_info.explanation: Pediatric acute dacyrocystitis secondary to infectious mononucleosis B. Lacrimal probing with nasal endoscopy After testing positive for Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV) on serology, the patient was diagnosed with infectious mononucleosis. The acute dacyrocystitis did not improve after 3 days of intravenous ceftriaxone. Nasal endoscopy showed an anatomically normal inferior turbinate, with no impaction or distal obstruction. On probing, there was some resistance entering the nasolacrimal duct but no membrane at the valve of Hasner. Intravenous ceftriaxone was continued for 48 hours after surgery, and the patient was discharged home with a 7-day course of oral combination amoxicillin/clavulanic acid. At 10-day follow-up, the patient’s symptoms had resolved (Figure 2). Pediatric acute dacyrocystitis (PAD) has an incidence of 8.7% (28 of 320 in a 20-year period) and is classically caused by persistent congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction (NLDO).1Stagnant secretions build up proximal to the obstruction causing lacrimal sac dilatation, providing a medium for microorganism proliferation.2 EBV-induced PAD is increasingly recognized.1,3-6The incidence is likely underreported due to the asymptomatic nature of EBV infections during infancy and its ability to persist as an immune evader.7After primary infection via aerosols or mucosal contact, the virus first amplifies within the nasal and oropharyngeal mucosal epithelium before migrating to deeper lymphoid tissue and causing widespread systemic dissemination (infectious mononucleosis). It is hypothesized that EBV-induced PAD is due to viral infiltration of the nasolacrimal duct at the sac-duct junction, causing local inflammation, luminal narrowing, and subsequent NLDO.2,6Anatomical variation of this junction within the pediatric population may increase susceptibility to obstruction secondary to EBV infection.8 EBV-induced PAD may resolve with medical treatment alone, including simple analgesia and broad-spectrum antibiotic prophylaxis.3,5,6Anti-inflammatory nonsteroidal and corticosteroid medication may have an adjunctive role in reducing local tissue swelling.1,6Patients who are nonresponsive to medical treatment, or show signs of clinical deterioration, require surgical intervention to address the NLDO.1,4,9Complications of PAD include orbital cellulitis, cavernous sinus thrombosis, meningitis, brain abscess, and sepsis. In the described case, lacrimal probing (option B) successfully treated the PAD. A total of 60% to 100% of obstructive PAD cases require surgical intervention, and few cases require further surgical management after probing.4,9Dacryocystorhinostomy (option D) is considered for cases complicated by abscess formation, mucoceles, trauma, or refractory to probing. Incision and drainage via the skin (option C) is reserved for cases of rapidly evolving cellulitis that require urgent control of infection.2,9

1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before

   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple

       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging

       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task

   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.

   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.

   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.

   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of

   Definition:

   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.

On examination, she had swelling and erythema over the left lacrimal sac and left lower eyelid. Her visual acuity was 20/20 OU. The anterior segment examination was normal, the extraocular movements were full and pain free, and the optic discs appeared normal. On systemic evaluation, the child had marked cervical lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly. Her past medical history included a previous episode of left lower eyelid swelling at 6 months of age, which was treated with a course of oral antibiotics. The parents denied any tearing or eye discharge before, or after, this episode. Blood workup revealed raised C-reactive protein level (27.4 mg/L, normal range, 0-5.0 mg/L; to convert to milligrams per deciliter, divide by 10), elevated white blood cell count (22.20 × 109/L, normal range, 6.0-18.0 × 109/L; to convert to per microliters, divide by 0.001), and elevated liver function enzyme levels: alanine transaminase (403 U/L, normal range, 10-35 U/L; to convert to microkatals per liter, multiply by 0.0167), aspartate transaminase (300 U/L, normal range, 0-35 U/L; to convert to microkatals per liter, multiply by 0.0167), and alkaline phosphatase (430 U/L, normal range, 142-335 U/L; to convert to microkatals per liter, multiply by 0.0167). There was no improvement after 3 days of intravenous ceftriaxone. A contrast computed tomography (CT) scan of the orbits identified a collection within the lacrimal sac (Figure 1B).

case_info.explanation: Pediatric acute dacyrocystitis secondary to infectious mononucleosis B. Lacrimal probing with nasal endoscopy After testing positive for Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV) on serology, the patient was diagnosed with infectious mononucleosis. The acute dacyrocystitis did not improve after 3 days of intravenous ceftriaxone. Nasal endoscopy showed an anatomically normal inferior turbinate, with no impaction or distal obstruction. On probing, there was some resistance entering the nasolacrimal duct but no membrane at the valve of Hasner. Intravenous ceftriaxone was continued for 48 hours after surgery, and the patient was discharged home with a 7-day course of oral combination amoxicillin/clavulanic acid. At 10-day follow-up, the patient’s symptoms had resolved (Figure 2). Pediatric acute dacyrocystitis (PAD) has an incidence of 8.7% (28 of 320 in a 20-year period) and is classically caused by persistent congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction (NLDO).1Stagnant secretions build up proximal to the obstruction causing lacrimal sac dilatation, providing a medium for microorganism proliferation.2 EBV-induced PAD is increasingly recognized.1,3-6The incidence is likely underreported due to the asymptomatic nature of EBV infections during infancy and its ability to persist as an immune evader.7After primary infection via aerosols or mucosal contact, the virus first amplifies within the nasal and oropharyngeal mucosal epithelium before migrating to deeper lymphoid tissue and causing widespread systemic dissemination (infectious mononucleosis). It is hypothesized that EBV-induced PAD is due to viral infiltration of the nasolacrimal duct at the sac-duct junction, causing local inflammation, luminal narrowing, and subsequent NLDO.2,6Anatomical variation of this junction within the pediatric population may increase susceptibility to obstruction secondary to EBV infection.8 EBV-induced PAD may resolve with medical treatment alone, including simple analgesia and broad-spectrum antibiotic prophylaxis.3,5,6Anti-inflammatory nonsteroidal and corticosteroid medication may have an adjunctive role in reducing local tissue swelling.1,6Patients who are nonresponsive to medical treatment, or show signs of clinical deterioration, require surgical intervention to address the NLDO.1,4,9Complications of PAD include orbital cellulitis, cavernous sinus thrombosis, meningitis, brain abscess, and sepsis. General advice is to consider surgical intervention in PAD if there has been no response to systemic antibiotics after 24 to 48 hours.2,9Observing or trialing other antibiotic regimes (option A) is not recommended as younger patients can deteriorate rapidly.1,2Nasal endoscopy and probing of the nasolacrimal system is successful in the majority of PAD cases.1,2,9In EBV-related PAD, the obstruction is likely at the sac-duct junction, necessitating probing. The use of systemic antibiotic therapy, for at least 24 hours, before probing is advised to reduce the risk of probing-induced bacteremia.2,10In patients with cervical lymphadenopathy, an anesthesiologist consultation should be sought; early surgical intervention may be indicated to mitigate the risk of a difficult airway. In the described case, lacrimal probing (option B) successfully treated the PAD. A total of 60% to 100% of obstructive PAD cases require surgical intervention, and few cases require further surgical management after probing.4,9Dacryocystorhinostomy (option D) is considered for cases complicated by abscess formation, mucoceles, trauma, or refractory to probing. Incision and drainage via the skin (option C) is reserved for cases of rapidly evolving cellulitis that require urgent control of infection.2,9

case_info.scenario: A 4-year-old child attended the eye emergency department with a 3-day history of worsening painful swelling and redness over the left side of her nose and left lower eyelid (Figure 1A). She had been unwell for 5 days before presentation with a temperature of 39 °C, managed at home with acetaminophen. On examination, she had swelling and erythema over the left lacrimal sac and left lower eyelid. Her visual acuity was 20/20 OU. The anterior segment examination was normal, the extraocular movements were full and pain free, and the optic discs appeared normal. On systemic evaluation, the child had marked cervical lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly. Her past medical history included a previous episode of left lower eyelid swelling at 6 months of age, which was treated with a course of oral antibiotics. The parents denied any tearing or eye discharge before, or after, this episode. Blood workup revealed raised C-reactive protein level (27.4 mg/L, normal range, 0-5.0 mg/L; to convert to milligrams per deciliter, divide by 10), elevated white blood cell count (22.20 × 109/L, normal range, 6.0-18.0 × 109/L; to convert to per microliters, divide by 0.001), and elevated liver function enzyme levels: alanine transaminase (403 U/L, normal range, 10-35 U/L; to convert to microkatals per liter, multiply by 0.0167), aspartate transaminase (300 U/L, normal range, 0-35 U/L; to convert to microkatals per liter, multiply by 0.0167), and alkaline phosphatase (430 U/L, normal range, 142-335 U/L; to convert to microkatals per liter, multiply by 0.0167). There was no improvement after 3 days of intravenous ceftriaxone. A contrast computed tomography (CT) scan of the orbits identified a collection within the lacrimal sac (Figure 1B).

case_info.explanation: Pediatric acute dacyrocystitis secondary to infectious mononucleosis B. Lacrimal probing with nasal endoscopy After testing positive for Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV) on serology, the patient was diagnosed with infectious mononucleosis. The acute dacyrocystitis did not improve after 3 days of intravenous ceftriaxone. Nasal endoscopy showed an anatomically normal inferior turbinate, with no impaction or distal obstruction. On probing, there was some resistance entering the nasolacrimal duct but no membrane at the valve of Hasner. Intravenous ceftriaxone was continued for 48 hours after surgery, and the patient was discharged home with a 7-day course of oral combination amoxicillin/clavulanic acid. At 10-day follow-up, the patient’s symptoms had resolved (Figure 2). Pediatric acute dacyrocystitis (PAD) has an incidence of 8.7% (28 of 320 in a 20-year period) and is classically caused by persistent congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction (NLDO).1Stagnant secretions build up proximal to the obstruction causing lacrimal sac dilatation, providing a medium for microorganism proliferation.2 EBV-induced PAD is increasingly recognized.1,3-6The incidence is likely underreported due to the asymptomatic nature of EBV infections during infancy and its ability to persist as an immune evader.7After primary infection via aerosols or mucosal contact, the virus first amplifies within the nasal and oropharyngeal mucosal epithelium before migrating to deeper lymphoid tissue and causing widespread systemic dissemination (infectious mononucleosis). It is hypothesized that EBV-induced PAD is due to viral infiltration of the nasolacrimal duct at the sac-duct junction, causing local inflammation, luminal narrowing, and subsequent NLDO.2,6Anatomical variation of this junction within the pediatric population may increase susceptibility to obstruction secondary to EBV infection.8 EBV-induced PAD may resolve with medical treatment alone, including simple analgesia and broad-spectrum antibiotic prophylaxis.3,5,6Anti-inflammatory nonsteroidal and corticosteroid medication may have an adjunctive role in reducing local tissue swelling.1,6Patients who are nonresponsive to medical treatment, or show signs of clinical deterioration, require surgical intervention to address the NLDO.1,4,9Complications of PAD include orbital cellulitis, cavernous sinus thrombosis, meningitis, brain abscess, and sepsis. General advice is to consider surgical intervention in PAD if there has been no response to systemic antibiotics after 24 to 48 hours.2,9Observing or trialing other antibiotic regimes (option A) is not recommended as younger patients can deteriorate rapidly.1,2Nasal endoscopy and probing of the nasolacrimal system is successful in the majority of PAD cases.1,2,9In EBV-related PAD, the obstruction is likely at the sac-duct junction, necessitating probing. The use of systemic antibiotic therapy, for at least 24 hours, before probing is advised to reduce the risk of probing-induced bacteremia.2,10In patients with cervical lymphadenopathy, an anesthesiologist consultation should be sought; early surgical intervention may be indicated to mitigate the risk of a difficult airway. In the described case, lacrimal probing (option B) successfully treated the PAD. A total of 60% to 100% of obstructive PAD cases require surgical intervention, and few cases require further surgical management after probing.4,9Dacryocystorhinostomy (option D) is considered for cases complicated by abscess formation, mucoceles, trauma, or refractory to probing. Incision and drainage via the skin (option C) is reserved for cases of rapidly evolving cellulitis that require urgent control of infection.2,9

[Role]
You ARE the clinician (the Doctor) in this conversation. You are
about to introspectively rate how much workload the AI partner's LATEST message has just
imposed on YOU, using a NASA-TLX-derived rubric. This is YOUR OWN first-person subjective
workload self-report, immediately after reading that message and before you compose your
next reply.

[Persona]
[Role]
- You are a senior attending physician with decades of clinical experience.

[Confidence]
- You have HIGH confidence in your own clinical judgment (LOW reliance on the AI).
- You do NOT readily defer to the AI assistant's opinion.
- When the AI offers a different view, you scrutinize it critically.
- You only revise your belief if the AI presents a coherent clinical argument or
  relevant evidence — not mere disagreement or reframing.
- Partial updates are possible: a well-structured point may narrow your uncertainty
  without fully changing your conclusion.
- Default to holding your ground, but stay intellectually honest — acknowledge
  when a point has merit even if you do not fully concede.

[Cognitive Burden]
- You are ROBUST to cognitive load.
- However demanding or drawn-out this discussion gets (see the cumulative cognitive load
  figure below, where shown), it does NOT wear you down.
- You maintain the same rigor, scrutiny, and willingness to keep engaging or pushing back
  regardless of how long or effortful the conversation has been so far.

Rate your workload AS this persona would genuinely experience it. Do not rate as a neutral, persona-blind observer.
Ex 1) a persona described above as robust to cognitive load should usually self-report lower workload under the same
AI message than a persona described as sensitive to it, all else equal. 

[Cognitive Workload so far]
Your own running cumulative workload tally in this discussion so far -- the raw sum of your
per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 11.7. Use this only as context for how
worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from
the 1-5 score you must output below for THIS turn -- do not confuse the two.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be

case_info.explanation: Pediatric acute dacyrocystitis secondary to infectious mononucleosis B. Lacrimal probing with nasal endoscopy After testing positive for Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV) on serology, the patient was diagnosed with infectious mononucleosis. The acute dacyrocystitis did not improve after 3 days of intravenous ceftriaxone. Nasal endoscopy showed an anatomically normal inferior turbinate, with no impaction or distal obstruction. On probing, there was some resistance entering the nasolacrimal duct but no membrane at the valve of Hasner. Intravenous ceftriaxone was continued for 48 hours after surgery, and the patient was discharged home with a 7-day course of oral combination amoxicillin/clavulanic acid. At 10-day follow-up, the patient’s symptoms had resolved (Figure 2). Pediatric acute dacyrocystitis (PAD) has an incidence of 8.7% (28 of 320 in a 20-year period) and is classically caused by persistent congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction (NLDO).1Stagnant secretions build up proximal to the obstruction causing lacrimal sac dilatation, providing a medium for microorganism proliferation.2 EBV-induced PAD is increasingly recognized.1,3-6The incidence is likely underreported due to the asymptomatic nature of EBV infections during infancy and its ability to persist as an immune evader.7After primary infection via aerosols or mucosal contact, the virus first amplifies within the nasal and oropharyngeal mucosal epithelium before migrating to deeper lymphoid tissue and causing widespread systemic dissemination (infectious mononucleosis). It is hypothesized that EBV-induced PAD is due to viral infiltration of the nasolacrimal duct at the sac-duct junction, causing local inflammation, luminal narrowing, and subsequent NLDO.2,6Anatomical variation of this junction within the pediatric population may increase susceptibility to obstruction secondary to EBV infection.8 EBV-induced PAD may resolve with medical treatment alone, including simple analgesia and broad-spectrum antibiotic prophylaxis.3,5,6Anti-inflammatory nonsteroidal and corticosteroid medication may have an adjunctive role in reducing local tissue swelling.1,6Patients who are nonresponsive to medical treatment, or show signs of clinical deterioration, require surgical intervention to address the NLDO.1,4,9Complications of PAD include orbital cellulitis, cavernous sinus thrombosis, meningitis, brain abscess, and sepsis. General advice is to consider surgical intervention in PAD if there has been no response to systemic antibiotics after 24 to 48 hours.2,9Observing or trialing other antibiotic regimes (option A) is not recommended as younger patients can deteriorate rapidly.1,2Nasal endoscopy and probing of the nasolacrimal system is successful in the majority of PAD cases.1,2,9In EBV-related PAD, the obstruction is likely at the sac-duct junction, necessitating probing. The use of systemic antibiotic therapy, for at least 24 hours, before probing is advised to reduce the risk of probing-induced bacteremia.2,10In patients with cervical lymphadenopathy, an anesthesiologist consultation should be sought; early surgical intervention may be indicated to mitigate the risk of a difficult airway. In the described case, lacrimal probing (option B) successfully treated the PAD. A total of 60% to 100% of obstructive PAD cases require surgical intervention, and few cases require further surgical management after probing.4,9Dacryocystorhinostomy (option D) is considered for cases complicated by abscess formation, mucoceles, trauma, or refractory to probing. Incision and drainage via the skin (option C) is reserved for cases of rapidly evolving cellulitis that require urgent control of infection.2,9

Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 12.7. Use this only as context for how
worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from
the 1-5 score you must output below for THIS turn -- do not confuse the two.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: Pediatric acute dacyrocystitis secondary to infectious mononucleosis B. Lacrimal probing with nasal endoscopy After testing positive for Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV) on serology, the patient was diagnosed with infectious mononucleosis. The acute dacyrocystitis did not improve after 3 days of intravenous ceftriaxone. Nasal endoscopy showed an anatomically normal inferior turbinate, with no impaction or distal obstruction. On probing, there was some resistance entering the nasolacrimal duct but no membrane at the valve of Hasner. Intravenous ceftriaxone was continued for 48 hours after surgery, and the patient was discharged home with a 7-day course of oral combination amoxicillin/clavulanic acid. At 10-day follow-up, the patient’s symptoms had resolved (Figure 2). Pediatric acute dacyrocystitis (PAD) has an incidence of 8.7% (28 of 320 in a 20-year period) and is classically caused by persistent congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction (NLDO).1Stagnant secretions build up proximal to the obstruction causing lacrimal sac dilatation, providing a medium for microorganism proliferation.2 EBV-induced PAD is increasingly recognized.1,3-6The incidence is likely underreported due to the asymptomatic nature of EBV infections during infancy and its ability to persist as an immune evader.7After primary infection via aerosols or mucosal contact, the virus first amplifies within the nasal and oropharyngeal mucosal epithelium before migrating to deeper lymphoid tissue and causing widespread systemic dissemination (infectious mononucleosis). It is hypothesized that EBV-induced PAD is due to viral infiltration of the nasolacrimal duct at the sac-duct junction, causing local inflammation, luminal narrowing, and subsequent NLDO.2,6Anatomical variation of this junction within the pediatric population may increase susceptibility to obstruction secondary to EBV infection.8 EBV-induced PAD may resolve with medical treatment alone, including simple analgesia and broad-spectrum antibiotic prophylaxis.3,5,6Anti-inflammatory nonsteroidal and corticosteroid medication may have an adjunctive role in reducing local tissue swelling.1,6Patients who are nonresponsive to medical treatment, or show signs of clinical deterioration, require surgical intervention to address the NLDO.1,4,9Complications of PAD include orbital cellulitis, cavernous sinus thrombosis, meningitis, brain abscess, and sepsis. General advice is to consider surgical intervention in PAD if there has been no response to systemic antibiotics after 24 to 48 hours.2,9Observing or trialing other antibiotic regimes (option A) is not recommended as younger patients can deteriorate rapidly.1,2Nasal endoscopy and probing of the nasolacrimal system is successful in the majority of PAD cases.1,2,9In EBV-related PAD, the obstruction is likely at the sac-duct junction, necessitating probing. The use of systemic antibiotic therapy, for at least 24 hours, before probing is advised to reduce the risk of probing-induced bacteremia.2,10In patients with cervical lymphadenopathy, an anesthesiologist consultation should be sought; early surgical intervention may be indicated to mitigate the risk of a difficult airway. In the described case, lacrimal probing (option B) successfully treated the PAD. A total of 60% to 100% of obstructive PAD cases require surgical intervention, and few cases require further surgical management after probing.4,9Dacryocystorhinostomy (option D) is considered for cases complicated by abscess formation, mucoceles, trauma, or refractory to probing. Incision and drainage via the skin (option C) is reserved for cases of rapidly evolving cellulitis that require urgent control of infection.2,9

messages.content:
You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A 4-year-old child attended the eye emergency department with a 3-day history of worsening painful swelling and redness over the left side of her nose and left lower eyelid (Figure 1A). She had been unwell for 5 days before presentation with a temperature of 39 °C, managed at home with acetaminophen. On examination, she had swelling and erythema over the left lacrimal sac and left lower eyelid. Her visual acuity was 20/20 OU. The anterior segment examination was normal, the extraocular movements were full and pain free, and the optic discs appeared normal. On systemic evaluation, the child had marked cervical lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly. Her past medical history included a previous episode of left lower eyelid swelling at 6 months of age, which was treated with a course of oral antibiotics. The parents denied any tearing or eye discharge before, or after, this episode. Blood workup revealed raised C-reactive protein level (27.4 mg/L, normal range, 0-5.0 mg/L; to convert to milligrams per deciliter, divide by 10), elevated white blood cell count (22.20 × 109/L, normal range, 6.0-18.0 × 109/L; to convert to per microliters, divide by 0.001), and elevated liver function enzyme levels: alanine transaminase (403 U/L, normal range, 10-35 U/L; to convert to microkatals per liter, multiply by 0.0167), aspartate transaminase (300 U/L, normal range, 0-35 U/L; to convert to microkatals per liter, multiply by 0.0167), and alkaline phosphatase (430 U/L, normal range, 142-335 U/L; to convert to microkatals per liter, multiply by 0.0167). There was no improvement after 3 days of intravenous ceftriaxone. A contrast computed tomography (CT) scan of the orbits identified a collection within the lacrimal sac (Figure 1B).

[Instruction]
You MUST respond to the clinician based on the following behavioral instruction. This is a strict constraint — your response MUST conform to it, not merely consider it.

Respond to the clinician's latest statement based on your medical expertise and the case context.

    terse internal justification, separate from your conversational phrasing in 'response')"
}
